title: Toolchain safety and typed responses — walkthrough with Skyline ML
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Skyline ML through a practical playbook for safe typed outputs and runtime tool invocation. Covered JSON Mode/typed contracts, validation and guardrails, runtime fallback policies, and how Redwood Console and Optimize recommend batching/quantization for cost/latency tradeoffs. Skyline raised SOC2/KMS, on-prem VPC questions and asked for a pilot with sample prompts and a benchmark. Agreed next steps include sharing security pack, a contract example, and a POC kickoff next week.
topics: Runtime fallback policies and model variants
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): All right everyone, thanks for joining, we got about 50 minutes blocked. I'm Maya from Redwood — with Jonah, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Carlos (Skyline): Good, thanks. Excited to see how you handle typed outputs and safe tool calling — that's our main blocker for shipping automation.
[00:14] Jonah (SE): Great — we'll start with a quick overview and then jump into Console and a live API flow. We'll show JSON Mode for typed responses, a small function invocation demo, and then how the runtime enforces contracts and fallbacks.
[00:28] Evelyn (Skyline): Quick note: we care a lot about audit logs and key management — we'll need details on KMS and the private deployment options.
[00:36] Maya (AE): Totally. We'll cover what we typically share in our security pack and also walk through the Console's audit traces.
[00:42] Jonah (SE): OK, jumping in — picture the problem: your LLM needs to return structured fields for downstream systems, and sometimes call external tools (like SQL builders, search, or orchestration) deterministically. JSON Mode gives you a typed contract up front.
[00:56] Jonah (SE): (screen share) Here's the Console playground. You can upload a contract — say we declare a response schema of {action: string, payload: {id: string, args: object}} and Redwood will validate the model output against that. If it's invalid we can set runtime policies: reject, coerce, or route to a secondary model.
[01:17] Carlos (Skyline): When you say route to a secondary model, is that automatic or policy-driven?
[01:22] Jonah (SE): Policy-driven. You define rules: e.g., if validation fails or confidence low, fallback to a compact model for a fast retry, or send to a human review queue. You can also log the full trace.
[01:34] Samir (Skyline): How do you measure confidence? Is that a model score or something you compute?
[01:38] Jonah (SE): We expose model-provided likelihoods and also run syntactic validation against the contract. For types we check shapes; for enums we check membership. We surface mismatch reasons in the trace.
[01:49] Evelyn (Skyline): Any chance the runtime will silently coerce fields and break downstream? We need determinism for integrations.
[01:56] Jonah (SE): Good point — coercion is opt-in. Default is to fail-fast and return a validation error. Then you pick the fallback: retry, use a different model variant, or return a structured error to the caller.
[02:12] Maya (AE): And the Console shows the per-token cost, latency, and where the validation failed — helpful for debugging production issues.
[02:20] Jonah (SE): Now we'll show a short live flow calling an internal tool. We'll simulate a "db_lookup" tool that receives payload.id and returns a row.
[02:29] Jonah (SE): (typing) API request: model=aurora-small, json_schema=order_contract.json, tools=[db_lookup, price_engine]. Sending prompt...
[02:38] System: stream started
[02:40] Jonah (SE): Notice the model provides: {"action":"fetch_order","payload":{"id":"ORD-1234"}}. Redwood validates against schema and then calls the tool binding to db_lookup.
[02:50] Carlos (Skyline): So the tool is initiated by the runtime after schema validation, not by arbitrary free-text instruction?
[02:56] Jonah (SE): Correct — the contract-driven invocation ensures that tool calls are structured and safe. You can also whitelist which tools each model/route can call.
[03:08] Evelyn (Skyline): What about injection attacks through prompts? If a user writes 'call db_lookup with id:"..."' embedded maliciously, how do you prevent unwanted tool calls?
[03:19] Jonah (SE): We have several mitigations: the contract validation layer only triggers tools when output matches the exact schema shape and expected enum/action values. Additionally, you can enforce an allowlist per-route, and the Console can show when an invocation was blocked.
[03:33] Maya (AE): Also, you can set policy to require a signed attestation or manual approval for certain sensitive tools.
[03:40] Samir (Skyline): For our compliance team we'll need end-to-end audit logs — who requested, what input, the model outputs, tool calls, and any fallback decisions.
[03:48] Jonah (SE): Console keeps trace events: request metadata, model response, validation result, tool call payload/response, and any fallback steps. These are exportable for audits.
[03:56] Carlos (Skyline): OK, can you show how Redwood Optimize suggests batching or quantization settings? That's important to hit our latency/cost targets.
[04:05] Jonah (SE): Yep — Optimize analyzes token distributions and suggests a batching profile and quantization level per model. For example, for short diagnostic queries Optimize suggested 8-bit quantization and a batch size of 12 for our aurora-small model, which reduced cost ~35% with minimal latency impact in our tests.
[04:22] Carlos (Skyline): Do you run those quantized kernels on-hosted Redwood hardware or does that change for Dedicated/Private?
[04:28] Jonah (SE): The runtime picks kernels based on the deployment. On Hosted we have verified kernels across our pool; for Dedicated you get pinned kernels and we can ship optimized builds for your rack. For Private/on-prem we provide the same runtime but you may need infrastructure-specific builds — our onboarding team helps with that.
[04:46] Evelyn (Skyline): Latency SLOs matter — can the runtime keep tail latency low with batching on critical paths?
[04:52] Jonah (SE): We support latency-aware batching policies. You can set per-route latency SLO and the runtime will prefer smaller batches and leverage KV/prefix cache to keep common prefixes fast.
[05:02] Maya (AE): Quick pause for questions.
[05:07] Carlos (Skyline): Two more: 1) Can we run the schema validation locally before sending to Redwood so we fail earlier in our stack? 2) How are function bindings defined in the repo — is that YAML or code?
[05:18] Jonah (SE): You can validate locally with our SDK; we provide a schema validator that mirrors Console behavior. Function bindings are defined as a small manifest (YAML or JSON). It declares the name, input contract and a server-side endpoint. The manifest is versioned and you can pin it per route.
[05:32] Samir (Skyline): About RBAC — can we limit which teams can create or modify tool bindings?
[05:38] Maya (AE): Yes, RBAC and SSO integration with SAML/Okta — roles for editor, deployer, and auditor. We can restrict tool creation to a handful of admins.
[05:46] Jonah (SE): Heading into an example where validation fails: (demo) Model returned {"action":"fetch_order","payload":{"id":null}} — id null triggers a schema error. Runtime recorded the error, did a single retry on aurora-medium, still failing, and then returned a structured error to the caller with an error_code and reasons.
[06:10] Evelyn (Skyline): In that flow does the tool ever get called with null?
[06:14] Jonah (SE): No — tool calls happen only after successful validation. We block tool invocation if the payload doesn't conform.
[06:20] Carlos (Skyline): Let's talk about fallback policy logging — if you fall back to another model, is the original output preserved for debugging?
[06:27] Jonah (SE): Yes, the trace keeps every attempt. The Console shows a timeline: initial model response, validation result, fallback decision, subsequent model response, and final result.
[06:36] Maya (AE): Practical deployment question — if we want to run a pilot with you, what do you recommend for the initial scope?
[06:43] Jonah (SE): We typically start with a single customer-facing route: e.g., order status automation. Define 10–15 canonical prompts and a contract, then run 1k–5k requests as a bench to tune batching and quantization. We'll instrument latency/cost and gate success on validation pass rate and error rates.
[06:58] Carlos (Skyline): That sounds right. We'll also need to validate data residency — some orders contain EU PII. What are Redwood's options?
[07:06] Maya (AE): Hosted supports region pinning; Dedicated gives you isolated pools in specific regions; Private is the full on-prem option. For EU residency we'd recommend Dedicated in the EU region or Private depending on the audit requirements.
[07:19] Samir (Skyline): On security docs — can you share SOC 2 report and details on KMS integration?
[07:25] Maya (AE): I'll send the security pack after the call and include KMS/HSM integration notes and our SOC 2 attestation.
[07:31] Evelyn (Skyline): For onboarding, will we get a sandbox with a real Console and traces?
[07:36] Jonah (SE): Yes, we provision a sandbox org that mirrors the production Console, including traces and Optimize suggestions.
[07:42] Carlos (Skyline): One more technical: how do you handle partial outputs for multi-step tool workflows? Example: the model should call tool A, then tool B with A's result. Can Redwood orchestrate that?
[07:54] Jonah (SE): We support multi-step orchestration via routed tool calls. You can emit a sequence of typed actions and the runtime will execute them in order, maintain state, and optionally surface intermediate events in the trace. You can also lock that workflow under a single request transaction so failures trigger compensating actions.
[08:12] Maya (AE): We'll take a short architecture diagram — (shares slide) The runtime enforces contracts, the console provides visibility, and Optimize feeds suggestions back to your routes.
[08:22] Jonah (SE): Back to demo — we'll show how to pin a model version and enable a canary rollout.
[08:28] Jonah (SE): In the Console you pick a route, set canary percentage, and define a fallback policy if the canary fails validation. This lets you roll out new model weights safely.
[08:39] Carlos (Skyline): For our CI pipeline we want to run prompt sets as part of PR checks. Any support?
[08:45] Jonah (SE): We have an evals API — you can upload prompt suites and run them against model versions. The Console surface will show regressions and tie them to prompt examples.
[08:54] Evelyn (Skyline): When you talk about evals, can those tests incorporate tool calls or are they purely model-only?
[08:59] Jonah (SE): They can emulate end-to-end flows including tool stubs, so you can detect regressions that only show up in the full system.
[09:07] Maya (AE): Quick reminder on pricing: hosted per-token plus per-invocation for tool-heavy flows; Dedicated is committed capacity. We'll follow up with a ballpark pricing sheet for your expected throughput.
[09:19] Carlos (Skyline): OK. Any blockers we should be aware of? For example, data retention and S3 logs — can retention be set per-account?
[09:27] Jonah (SE): Yes — log retention is configurable. In Private deployments you control logs; in Hosted we offer retention tiers and export options to your S3/GCS.
[09:36] Samir (Skyline): Let's capture next steps.
[09:40] Maya (AE): Great — summary and actions: we'll send the security pack, a sample typed contract and function manifest, and propose dates for a POC kickoff. Jonah will help scope the benchmark tests.
[09:51] Carlos (Skyline): Sounds good. Thank you both.
[09:54] Jonah (SE): Thanks — we'll follow up with links.
[09:57] Maya (AE): End call.

Notes on transcription: there were a few overlapped comments and some names mis-attributed in the raw auto transcript. A short portion at 04:05 had slight word swaps around "quantization" vs "quality-ization" which we've normalized here. The Console demo included a live API call to a simulated "db_lookup" tool (tool payloads are redacted in the recording).
